warmup.q: static Supplier<String> greeter() { return () -> "hello"; }. What does greeter() == greeter() print on a current JDK?
options: false: every lambda expression creates a new object
true: the lambda captures nothing, so its call site hands back one shared object
It doesn't compile: you can't compare lambdas with ==
true, but only after the JIT has compiled greeter
warmup.why: The lambda is an invokedynamic call site. The first time it runs, LambdaMetafactory links it, and for a lambda that captures nothing, the linked target returns the same instance every time. It prints true from the first call, before the JIT is involved. A capturing lambda such as s -> s + extra gets a new object each time the expression is evaluated. The section on taking a lambda apart shows both in one demo.

opening:
Most cues in a prompt book are complete: "LX 14 GO". A few say only "ask the director". On the first night, the stage manager reaches that cue and asks. The director decides, and the answer is written into the margin. From then on, the stage manager reads the margin and never asks again, which suits the director fine.

The JVM has a cue like that, and it's the one javap couldn't finish for us in the last lesson: invokedynamic. It's behind every lambda you write, and behind every string you build with +. The first time such an instruction runs, library code decides what it calls, and the answer is kept for good.

It's easy to guess wrong about what that costs. Many people picture a lambda as a small inner class, or believe each lambda allocates on every call. So they avoid lambdas where they're cheap, and miss the allocation where it's real. In this lesson, we'll watch a call site get linked once, take a lambda apart, see string + and records use the same trick, and then do the linking by hand. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We met the cue that says "ask the director": an invokedynamic whose bootstrap method decides once and writes the answer in ink. Behind it sat a private body method, a hidden $$Lambda class, a fill-in-the-blanks recipe for strings, and a description for each record.

Now run javap -c -p on a class of yours that uses lambdas, and read each call-site type. Any that starts with your own class captures this, and any with parameters allocates each time it runs.

Next, we'll put a stand-in in front of an object: a class the JDK writes while your program runs. What does that class look like, and what does each call through it cost?

sections.h: invokedynamic: a call whose target is decided once, at first use
sections.html:
Every other call instruction names its target. invokestatic StackDemo.seconds:(JI)J calls exactly that method, like a cue that says "LX 14 GO". invokedynamic names only a method name, a type, and a bootstrap method: a method that will decide the target the first time the instruction runs. Here is the method reference IndyTour::add in javap -c -p, and its entry from javap -v, on JDK 25:

invokedynamic #15,  0   // InvokeDynamic #2:applyAsInt:()Ljava/util/function/IntBinaryOperator;

BootstrapMethods:
  2: REF_invokeStatic java/lang/invoke/LambdaMetafactory.metafactory:(...)Ljava/lang/invoke/CallSite;
    Method arguments:
      (II)I
      REF_invokeStatic workbench/bytecode/l03/IndyTour.add:(II)I
      (II)I

Read the type ()IntBinaryOperator from the point of view of the code around it: take nothing off the operand stack, and put an IntBinaryOperator on it. How the instruction gets one isn't written anywhere in your class file.

That's the cue that says "ask the director", and the bootstrap method is the director. The first time the instruction runs, the JVM calls the bootstrap method with four things. They are a Lookup for your class (an object that carries your class's access rights), the name, the type, and the static arguments listed above.

The bootstrap method returns a CallSite, an object that holds a target of exactly that type. The target is a method handle, a typed reference to a method that the JVM can call directly, much like a function pointer. The JVM links the instruction to the call site. From then on, every run calls the target directly, and the bootstrap method never runs again for that instruction. The answer is in the margin, and the director gets the rest of the run off.

LambdaMetafactory, the JDK's bootstrap method for lambdas, and StringConcatFactory, its bootstrap method for string +, both return a ConstantCallSite, whose target can never change. Here the picture needs one correction. A real margin note is in pencil, and a director can change their mind. A ConstantCallSite is written in ink, and that's what lets the JIT compile straight through it, as if the instruction had named its target all along. For languages that do need to relink later, the JDK has MutableCallSite, and the Try it below relinks one by hand.

invokedynamic arrived in Java 7, for other languages that run on the JVM, and javac first used it for lambdas in Java 8. It moves a decision out of your class files and into the JDK. The bytecode says "join an int and a String with this recipe". The JDK you run on decides how, so a newer JDK can do it better, and your old class files pick that up without being recompiled.

An invokedynamic is linked once, at first use. After that, it's a direct call.

So the director is library code in the JDK. Let's see what it builds when the cue is a lambda.

try.title: Relink a call site by hand
steps: Read CallSiteDemo. It builds a MutableCallSite aimed at inSeconds, calls through its dynamicInvoker(), changes the target to inMinutes, and calls again with the same 120.
Predict the three lines it prints, then run it (or the Kotlin twin).

code.title: CallSiteDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.bytecode.l03; import java.lang.invoke.ConstantCallSite; import java.lang.invoke.MethodHandle; import java.lang.invoke.MethodHandles; import java.lang.invoke.MethodType; import java.lang.invoke.MutableCallSite; /** A call site is a slot holding a target method handle. invokedynamic calls through one. */ public class CallSiteDemo { static String inSeconds(long s) { return s + " seconds"; } static String inMinutes(long s) { return s / 60 + " minutes"; } public static void main(String[] args) throws Throwable { MethodHandles.Lookup lookup = MethodHandles.lookup(); MethodType type = MethodType.methodType(String.class, long.class); MethodHandle inSeconds = lookup.findStatic(CallSiteDemo.class, "inSeconds", type); MethodHandle inMinutes = lookup.findStatic(CallSiteDemo.class, "inMinutes", type); MutableCallSite site = new MutableCallSite(inSeconds); MethodHandle invoker = site.dynamicInvoker(); // what an invokedynamic instruction would call through System.out.println("linked to inSeconds: " + (String) invoker.invokeExact(120L)); site.setTarget(inMinutes); // relink: same invoker, new target System.out.println("relinked to inMinutes: " + (String) invoker.invokeExact(120L)); ConstantCallSite fixed = new ConstantCallSite(inSeconds); // what lambdas and string concatenation get try { fixed.setTarget(inMinutes); } catch (UnsupportedOperationException e) { System.out.println("ConstantCallSite.setTarget -> UnsupportedOperationException: linked for good"); } } }

alt.title: CallSiteDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.bytecode.l03 import java.lang.invoke.ConstantCallSite import java.lang.invoke.MethodHandles import java.lang.invoke.MethodType import java.lang.invoke.MutableCallSite // A call site is a slot holding a target method handle. invokedynamic calls through one. object Formats { @JvmStatic fun inSeconds(s: Long) = "$s seconds" @JvmStatic fun inMinutes(s: Long) = "${s / 60} minutes" } fun main() { val lookup = MethodHandles.lookup() val type = MethodType.methodType(String::class.java, Long::class.javaPrimitiveType) val inSeconds = lookup.findStatic(Formats::class.java, "inSeconds", type) val inMinutes = lookup.findStatic(Formats::class.java, "inMinutes", type) val site = MutableCallSite(inSeconds) val invoker = site.dynamicInvoker() // what an invokedynamic instruction would call through println("linked to inSeconds: " + invoker.invoke(120L) as String) site.target = inMinutes // relink: same invoker, new target println("relinked to inMinutes: " + invoker.invoke(120L) as String) val fixed = ConstantCallSite(inSeconds) // what lambdas and string concatenation get try { fixed.target = inMinutes } catch (e: UnsupportedOperationException) { println("ConstantCallSite.setTarget -> UnsupportedOperationException: linked for good") } }

try.expect: linked to inSeconds: 120 seconds, then relinked to inMinutes: 2 minutes through the very same invoker, then a line saying ConstantCallSite.setTarget threw UnsupportedOperationException. An invokedynamic instruction calls through its call site the way the invoker does. Lambdas get the constant kind: written in ink, linked for good.

video.title: A lambda is a body method plus an invokedynamic that LambdaMetafactory links once

sections.h: Taking a lambda apart: a body method, plus a hidden class built at first use
sections.html:
The theatre's lighting cues run on seconds, and sometimes a whole sequence has to run a little late. delay(5) returns a function that adds 5 seconds to any cue time. javac turns that lambda into two things: a private method that holds the body, and an invokedynamic that produces the object:

Java
static IntUnaryOperator delay(int extra) {
    return s -> s + extra;               // a lambda that captures extra
}
Kotlin
fun delay(extra: Int): (Int) -> Int =
    { s -> s + extra }                   // a lambda that captures extra

Here is what javap showed for each compiler on JDK 25, trimmed to the lines that matter:

javac, IndyTour.class:
   1: invokedynamic #11,  0   // InvokeDynamic #1:applyAsInt:(I)Ljava/util/function/IntUnaryOperator;
  private static int lambda$delay$1(int, int);            // (extra, s): captured value first
  BootstrapMethods 1: LambdaMetafactory.metafactory
      (I)I
      REF_invokeStatic workbench/bytecode/l03/IndyTour.lambda$delay$1:(II)I
      (I)I

kotlinc, IndyTourKt.class:
   1: invokedynamic #44,  0   // InvokeDynamic #1:invoke:(I)Lkotlin/jvm/functions/Function1;
  private static final int delay$lambda$0(int, int);
  BootstrapMethods 1: LambdaMetafactory.metafactory
      (Ljava/lang/Object;)Ljava/lang/Object;
      REF_invokeStatic workbench/bytecode/l03/IndyTourKt.delay$lambda$0:(II)I
      (Ljava/lang/Integer;)Ljava/lang/Integer;

Read the call-site type as a factory: (I)IntUnaryOperator means "give me the captured int, and I'll give you an operator". To capture is to store a value from the surrounding code inside the lambda, here extra. The body method takes the captured values first, then the lambda's own parameter.

Then come the three static arguments. The first is the interface method's type after erasure, the compiler removing generic types, as in the generics track. The second is the body, and the third is the interface method's type as this lambda uses it. Kotlin's Function1.invoke is erased to (Object)Object, so the third argument, (Integer)Integer, tells the factory to insert the boxing and the casts.

At link time, LambdaMetafactory generates a class. On JDK 25 the demo printed its name as IndyTour$$Lambda/0x00000000a3080210. It's a hidden class, one defined with Lookup.defineHiddenClass (JDK 15) that no class loader can find by name, so Class.forName on that name throws ClassNotFoundException. It's also a nestmate of IndyTour, a class allowed to use IndyTour's private members, which is how it may call the private body. Since JDK 24, the JDK writes these classes with the ClassFile API that lesson 6 covers.

IndyTour shows the allocation rule in two lines of output:

captures nothing: same object both times? true
captures extra: same object? false, same class? true

A lambda that captures nothing is linked to one shared instance, so greeter() == greeter() is true, from the very first call. Two calls, one object. A capturing lambda gets a new object each time the lambda expression is evaluated, and all of those objects share one class. That's one small allocation each time delay(...) runs, not one per call of the operator it returns.

Kotlin compiles lambdas the same way, and has done so by default since Kotlin 2.0. The release notes list what you give up: such a lambda isn't serializable, and its toString() is less readable. Function references are different. In the Kotlin demo, ::addSeconds stored as (Int, Int) -> Int compiled to an ordinary generated class, IndyTourKt$main$ref$1, and isHidden printed false.

A lambda allocates once per evaluation if it captures, and never if it doesn't.

A lambda is one kind of question for the director. String + asks another.

try.title: Tour the lambdas
steps: Run IndyTour, then IndyTourKt. Compare the class names they print.
From labs/, run javap -c -p bytecode/build/classes/java/demo/workbench/bytecode/l03/IndyTour.class | grep -E 'invokedynamic|lambda' and match each invokedynamic to a line of source.
Do the same for bytecode/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/bytecode/l03/IndyTourKt.class, and run ls on that folder. Which Kotlin construct got a class file of its own?

code.title: IndyTour.java
code.html: package workbench.bytecode.l03; import java.util.function.IntBinaryOperator; import java.util.function.IntUnaryOperator; import java.util.function.Supplier; /** Lambdas, a method reference, string concatenation and a record: every one is an invokedynamic. */ public class IndyTour { record Cue(String name, int seconds) {} static int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; } static Supplier<String> greeter() { return () -> "hello"; } // captures nothing static IntUnaryOperator delay(int extra) { return s -> s + extra; } // captures extra public static void main(String[] args) { IntBinaryOperator ref = IndyTour::add; Class<?> c = ref.getClass(); System.out.println("method ref: " + ref.applyAsInt(90, 30) + ", class " + c.getName()); System.out.println("hidden: " + c.isHidden() + ", nestmate of IndyTour: " + (c.getNestHost() == IndyTour.class)); try { Class.forName(c.getName()); } catch (ClassNotFoundException e) { System.out.println("Class.forName(its name): ClassNotFoundException"); } System.out.println("captures nothing: same object both times? " + (greeter() == greeter())); IntUnaryOperator d5 = delay(5), d10 = delay(10); System.out.println("captures extra: same object? " + (d5 == d10) + ", same class? " + (d5.getClass() == d10.getClass())); Cue cue = new Cue("thunder", 90); System.out.println("concat: " + cue.seconds() + " s to " + cue.name() + ", record: " + cue); } }

alt.title: IndyTour.kt
alt.html: package workbench.bytecode.l03 // Lambdas, a function reference, a string template and a data class, compiled by kotlinc 2.4.21. data class KCue(val name: String, val seconds: Int) fun addSeconds(a: Int, b: Int) = a + b fun greeter(): () -> String = { "hello" } // captures nothing fun delay(extra: Int): (Int) -> Int = { s -> s + extra } // captures extra fun main() { val ref: (Int, Int) -> Int = ::addSeconds val c = ref.javaClass println("function ref: ${ref(90, 30)}, class ${c.name}") println("hidden: ${c.isHidden}") val lambda = greeter() println("lambda class ${lambda.javaClass.name}, hidden: ${lambda.javaClass.isHidden}") println("captures nothing: same object both times? ${greeter() === greeter()}") val d5 = delay(5) val d10 = delay(10) println("captures extra: same object? ${d5 === d10}, same class? ${d5.javaClass == d10.javaClass}") val cue = KCue("thunder", 90) println("template: ${cue.seconds} s to ${cue.name}, data class: $cue") }

try.expect: Java: IndyTour$$Lambda/0x..., hidden: true, a nestmate of IndyTour, Class.forName fails, same object both times? true for greeter, and same object? false, same class? true for delay. Kotlin: the lambdas print IndyTourKt$$Lambda/0x... and hidden: true, but the function reference prints IndyTourKt$main$ref$1 and hidden: false. That's the IndyTourKt$main$ref$1.class file in the folder. Both programs also contain several makeConcatWithConstants call sites, one for each string they build.

refs.title: What's new in Kotlin 2.0.0: lambdas via invokedynamic

sections.h: String concatenation, records and switches ask a bootstrap method too
sections.html:
Since JDK 9 (JEP 280), javac compiles + on strings to one invokedynamic per expression, linked by StringConcatFactory.makeConcatWithConstants. Before that, javac wrote a chain of StringBuilder calls into every class file, and that choice stayed frozen there. The constant parts now travel as a recipe, a fill-in-the-blanks line in which \u0001 marks each value to be filled in. Here's the last line of IndyTour in both languages:

Java
"concat: " + cue.seconds() + " s to " + cue.name() + ", record: " + cue
Kotlin
"template: ${cue.seconds} s to ${cue.name}, data class: $cue"

javac, IndyTour.class:
 195: invokestatic  #97    // Method java/lang/String.valueOf:(Ljava/lang/Object;)Ljava/lang/String;
 198: invokedynamic #103,  0   // InvokeDynamic #7:makeConcatWithConstants:(ILjava/lang/String;Ljava/lang/String;)Ljava/lang/String;
      BootstrapMethods 7, recipe: concat: \u0001 s to \u0001, record: \u0001

kotlinc, IndyTourKt.class:
 188: invokedynamic #147,  0   // InvokeDynamic #7:makeConcatWithConstants:(ILjava/lang/String;Lworkbench/bytecode/l03/KCue;)Ljava/lang/String;
      BootstrapMethods 7, recipe: template: \u0001 s to \u0001, data class: \u0001

The call-site type lists the values in order: an int, the cue's name and the cue. javac first turned the record into a String with String.valueOf, and kotlinc passed the data class object as it is. Kotlin templates compile this way when the JVM target is 9 or newer, which the labs use. With kotlinc's command-line default of Java 8, the same template becomes a StringBuilder chain, as lesson 2 found.

Records push the idea further. A record's toString, hashCode and equals are each a couple of instructions around an invokedynamic. The bootstrap is java.lang.runtime.ObjectMethods.bootstrap (JDK 16), and its static arguments describe the record:

ObjectMethods.bootstrap
  Method arguments:
    workbench/bytecode/l03/IndyTour$Cue
    name;seconds
    REF_getField workbench/bytecode/l03/IndyTour$Cue.name:Ljava/lang/String;
    REF_getField workbench/bytecode/l03/IndyTour$Cue.seconds:I

The JDK builds the three methods from that description the first time each is called. A Kotlin data class takes the other road: kotlinc writes the toString body itself, as getfield name, getfield seconds and a concatenation invokedynamic with the recipe KCue(name=\u0001, seconds=\u0001). Both print the same kind of text. The record carries a description, and the data class carries finished code.

Pattern-matching switch over a sealed type, one that lists all of its subtypes, compiles to invokedynamic typeSwitch, linked by java.lang.runtime.SwitchBootstraps. javac 21 and later also use a related form, condy (CONSTANT_Dynamic), for enum case labels in such a switch. A condy entry is a constant whose value a bootstrap method works out on first use. Same idea, for a value instead of a call.

String +, records and pattern switches all ask a bootstrap method. javap shows the recipe.

Every bootstrap method so far was called by the JVM. Nothing stops your code from calling one.

try.title: A record and a data class, side by side
steps: From labs/ (after running IndyTour and IndyTourKt once), run the two javap commands below.
In the record, find which bootstrap method its toString uses and the string that lists its components.
In the data class, find the recipe that toString passes to makeConcatWithConstants.

code.title: terminal
code.html: javap -v 'bytecode/build/classes/java/demo/workbench/bytecode/l03/IndyTour$Cue.class' | grep -A6 BootstrapMethods javap -v bytecode/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/bytecode/l03/KCue.class | grep -A3 BootstrapMethods

try.expect: The record's toString, hashCode and equals all use bootstrap 0, ObjectMethods.bootstrap, with the arguments IndyTour$Cue, name;seconds and two REF_getField handles. The data class has only a StringConcatFactory.makeConcatWithConstants bootstrap, with the recipe KCue(name=\u0001, seconds=\u0001). Its hashCode and equals are plain bytecode that kotlinc wrote.

sections.html:
A bootstrap method is an ordinary public static method, so your code can play the JVM and ask the director itself. That's today's lab. LambdaMetafactory.metafactory takes six arguments, and javap -v has already shown you all of them. Here it turns a static method banner(), which returns "curtain up in five minutes", into a Supplier<String>:

Java
CallSite site = LambdaMetafactory.metafactory(
        lookup,                                 // 1. caller: must be able to see the body
        "get",                                  // 2. interface method name
        methodType(Supplier.class),             // 3. factory type: captured values -> interface
        methodType(Object.class),               // 4. interface method type, erased
        lookup.findStatic(ByHandDemo.class, "banner", methodType(String.class)),  // 5. body
        methodType(String.class));              // 6. interface method type as this lambda uses it
Supplier<String> s = (Supplier<String>) site.getTarget().invoke();
Kotlin
val site = LambdaMetafactory.metafactory(
    lookup,                                     // 1. caller: must be able to see the body
    "get",                                      // 2. interface method name
    methodType(Supplier::class.java),           // 3. factory type: captured values -> interface
    methodType(Any::class.java),                // 4. interface method type, erased
    lookup.findStatic(Banners::class.java, "banner", methodType(String::class.java)),  // 5. body
    methodType(String::class.java),             // 6. interface method type as this lambda uses it
)
val s = site.target.invoke() as Supplier<String>

The JVM supplies arguments 1 to 3 from the call site, and the static arguments are 4 to 6. getTarget() is the factory. Calling it does what the invokedynamic instruction would do on every run: it takes the captured values and returns a lambda object. For a lambda that captures nothing, call the factory once and keep the result. For one that captures, keep the factory and call it once per object, which is the shape the lab tests for.

The generated class is a nestmate of the lookup's class, so the demo printed ByHandDemo$$Lambda/0x..., exactly like a lambda javac compiled. The Kotlin twin printed ByHandDemoKt$$Lambda/0x....

StringConcatFactory.makeConcatWithConstants(lookup, name, type, recipe) works the same way. The demo asks it for a (int, long)String handle with the recipe row \u0001 has \u0001 seats, calls it with 12 and 30, and gets row 12 has 30 seats. Both call sites came back as ConstantCallSite.

Why would you do this outside a lab? You rarely need to. Code that has a Method in hand at run time can turn it into an interface object once, and then call it as fast as a lambda. A serializer (code that turns objects into text or bytes) and a router (code that picks which method to call by name, while the program runs) are that kind of code. Doing the work once beats paying for Method.invoke, the reflective call, on every call.

Every call site in this lesson linked to a method that already existed. The next lesson's tool goes one step further: the JDK writes a whole new class, implementing any interface you name, while your program runs.

try.title: One lambda and one concatenation, by hand
steps: Read ByHandDemo. Match each of the six metafactory arguments to the javap -v listing in the first section.
Run it (or the Kotlin twin) and read the class and call-site names it prints.

code.title: ByHandDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.bytecode.l03; import java.lang.invoke.CallSite; import java.lang.invoke.LambdaMetafactory; import java.lang.invoke.MethodHandle; import java.lang.invoke.MethodHandles; import java.lang.invoke.MethodType; import java.lang.invoke.StringConcatFactory; import java.util.function.Supplier; import static java.lang.invoke.MethodType.methodType; /** The two bootstrap calls javac's invokedynamic would make, made by hand. */ public class ByHandDemo { static String banner() { return "curtain up in five minutes"; } @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") public static void main(String[] args) throws Throwable { MethodHandles.Lookup lookup = MethodHandles.lookup(); // 1. () -> banner() as a Supplier<String> CallSite site = LambdaMetafactory.metafactory( lookup, "get", // the interface method's name methodType(Supplier.class), // factory type: captures nothing methodType(Object.class), // Supplier.get() after erasure lookup.findStatic(ByHandDemo.class, "banner", methodType(String.class)), methodType(String.class)); // get() as this lambda returns it Supplier<String> s = (Supplier<String>) site.getTarget().invoke(); System.out.println(s.get() + " <- " + s.getClass().getName() + ", call site: " + site.getClass().getSimpleName()); // 2. "row " + row + " has " + count + " seats" CallSite concat = StringConcatFactory.makeConcatWithConstants( lookup, "concat", methodType(String.class, int.class, long.class), "row \u0001 has \u0001 seats"); MethodHandle mh = concat.getTarget(); System.out.println((String) mh.invokeExact(12, 30L) + " <- call site: " + concat.getClass().getSimpleName()); } }

alt.title: ByHandDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.bytecode.l03 import java.lang.invoke.LambdaMetafactory import java.lang.invoke.MethodHandles import java.lang.invoke.MethodType.methodType import java.lang.invoke.StringConcatFactory import java.util.function.Supplier object Banners { @JvmStatic fun banner() = "curtain up in five minutes" } // The two bootstrap calls an invokedynamic would make, made by hand from Kotlin. fun main() { val lookup = MethodHandles.lookup() // 1. () -> banner() as a Supplier<String> val site = LambdaMetafactory.metafactory( lookup, "get", // the interface method's name methodType(Supplier::class.java), // factory type: captures nothing methodType(Any::class.java), // Supplier.get() after erasure lookup.findStatic(Banners::class.java, "banner", methodType(String::class.java)), methodType(String::class.java), // get() as this lambda returns it ) @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") val s = site.target.invoke() as Supplier<String> println("${s.get()} <- ${s.javaClass.name}, call site: ${site.javaClass.simpleName}") // 2. "row " + row + " has " + count + " seats" val concat = StringConcatFactory.makeConcatWithConstants( lookup, "concat", methodType(String::class.java, Int::class.javaPrimitiveType, Long::class.javaPrimitiveType), "row \u0001 has \u0001 seats", ) println("${concat.target.invoke(12, 30L)} <- call site: ${concat.javaClass.simpleName}") }

try.expect: curtain up in five minutes <- ...ByHandDemo$$Lambda/0x..., call site: ConstantCallSite, then row 12 has 30 seats <- call site: ConstantCallSite. The lambda class is hidden and named after the lookup's class, exactly like a javac lambda. The Kotlin twin prints ByHandDemoKt$$Lambda.

compare.title: Lambdas and function references in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Cues.java
java.html: static int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; } IntBinaryOperator ref = Cues::add; // invokedynamic -> hidden Cues$$Lambda IntUnaryOperator plus5 = s -> s + 5; // invokedynamic, body in lambda$main$0 int extra = 10; IntUnaryOperator later = s -> s + extra; // invokedynamic with type (I)IntUnaryOperator String line = "delay " + extra + " s"; // invokedynamic makeConcatWithConstants

kotlin.title: Cues.kt
kotlin.html: fun add(a: Int, b: Int) = a + b val ref: (Int, Int) -> Int = ::add // a generated class (CuesKt$main$ref$1 style) val plus5: (Int) -> Int = { s -> s + 5 } // invokedynamic -> hidden CuesKt$$Lambda val extra = 10 val later: (Int) -> Int = { s -> s + extra } // invokedynamic with type (I)Function1 val line = "delay $extra s" // invokedynamic makeConcatWithConstants (target 9+)

compare.note: Both compilers send lambdas through LambdaMetafactory, so both get hidden $$Lambda classes, a shared instance when nothing is captured, and one class per lambda expression. Two real differences show up in javap. Kotlin's function types are generic interfaces (Function1<P, R>), so an (Int) -> Int boxes its Int through invoke(Object): Object, while Java's IntUnaryOperator stays with plain int. And in this track's kotlinc 2.4.21 build, a function reference such as ::add assigned to a function type compiled to an ordinary generated class instead of an invokedynamic. Kotlin's inline functions such as forEach and map avoid the lambda object entirely, which Java can't do.

steps.say: The show program fires a list of lighting cues, each shifted by an offset in seconds. lights is the object that talks to the lighting desk. Before you read on: does the lambda capture anything, and how often does it allocate?
steps.code: class CueRunner { private final Lights lights; void run(List<Cue> cues, int offset) { cues.forEach(c -> lights.fire(c.name(), c.seconds() + offset)); } }

alt.html: class KCueRunner(private val lights: KLights) { fun run(cues: List<KCue>, offset: Int) { cues.forEach { c -> lights.fire(c.name, c.seconds + offset) } } }

steps.say: Ask javap. This is what it printed for the Java class, compiled by JDK 25's javac. The call-site type lists the captured values: this, because lights is a field and is read through this, and the int offset. For the same reason, the body became an instance method rather than a static one.

So Java allocates one Consumer per call to run, once per list and not once per cue, and calls it once per element. The Kotlin version compiles to no lambda at all: forEach is an inline function, so kotlinc pasted the loop into run. Its bytecode is Iterable.iterator, hasNext, next and a direct KLights.fire. Store the same lambda in a val first, and Kotlin does what Java does. The comments show what javap printed for this version:
steps.code: fun runStored(cues: List<KCue>, offset: Int) { val fire: (KCue) -> Unit = { c -> lights.fire(c.name, c.seconds + offset) } cues.forEach(fire) } // 3. invokedynamic #92, 0 // InvokeDynamic #0:invoke:(LKCueRunner;I)Lkotlin/jvm/functions/Function1; // private static final kotlin.Unit runStored$lambda$0(KCueRunner, int, KCue);

alt.html: void runStored(List<Cue> cues, int offset) { Consumer<Cue> fire = c -> lights.fire(c.name(), c.seconds() + offset); cues.forEach(fire); } // 3. invokedynamic #23, 0 // InvokeDynamic #1:accept:(LCueRunner;I)Ljava/util/function/Consumer; // Java has no inline functions, so a lambda passed to forEach is always an object

steps.say: The verdict: one small object per list of cues is nothing next to driving the lighting desk, so leave the code as it is. The habit worth keeping is reading the call-site type. When it starts with your own class, the lambda holds this, which also keeps that object reachable for as long as the lambda lives.

lab.title: Build three lambdas and a concatenation by hand
steps: Run the tests once. All six fail with UnsupportedOperationException. HandMadeLambdas works with cue times in seconds, and its two body methods, addSeconds and addDelay, are already written.

Add private static final MethodHandles.Lookup LOOKUP = MethodHandles.lookup();. Write adder() with LambdaMetafactory.metafactory: name applyAsInt, factory type ()IntBinaryOperator, both interface types (II)I, and LOOKUP.findStatic(HandMadeLambdas.class, "addSeconds", ...). Invoke the factory once, store the object in a static field, and return it every time.

Write plusDelay(int). The factory type is (int)IntUnaryOperator, the interface types are (I)I, and the body is addDelay, whose first parameter receives the captured delay. Store the factory handle (site.getTarget()), not an object, and call (IntUnaryOperator) factory.invokeExact(delay) on each call.
Write lengthOf() with LOOKUP.findVirtual(String.class, "length", methodType(int.class)). The erased type is (Object)Object, and the instantiated type is (String)Integer.

Write countdown() with StringConcatFactory.makeConcatWithConstants(LOOKUP, "countdown", methodType(String.class, long.class, String.class), "\u0001 seconds to \u0001") and return the call site's target.
Run the tests until all six pass.
hints: Bootstrap methods throw checked exceptions. Wrap them once in a small helper that rethrows as ExceptionInInitializerError or IllegalStateException. Mind the order of your static fields: lesson 1's rule applies.

LambdaConversionException: Type mismatch usually means the instantiated type (the sixth argument) doesn't match the body's parameters after the captured ones. For plusDelay the body is (int, int)int, and the lambda's own part is (int)int.
invokeExact needs the exact static type: cast the result to IntUnaryOperator and pass an int. invoke is more forgiving if you get stuck.

drill.title: Spell out a metafactory call
drill.prompt: Close the page. Write the code that turns a static method static String banner() into a Supplier<String> with LambdaMetafactory.metafactory, without a lambda or a method reference. Label the six arguments. Then say which arguments the JVM supplies and which come from the BootstrapMethods table.

answer.html: MethodHandles.Lookup lookup = MethodHandles.lookup(); CallSite site = LambdaMetafactory.metafactory( lookup, // 1. caller (the JVM supplies it) "get", // 2. interface method name (JVM, from the call site) methodType(Supplier.class), // 3. factory type (JVM, from the call site) methodType(Object.class), // 4. erased interface type (static argument) lookup.findStatic(Owner.class, "banner", methodType(String.class)), // 5. body (static argument) methodType(String.class)); // 6. instantiated type (static argument) @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") Supplier<String> s = (Supplier<String>) site.getTarget().invoke();

alt.html: val lookup = MethodHandles.lookup() val site = LambdaMetafactory.metafactory( lookup, // 1. caller (the JVM supplies it) "get", // 2. interface method name (JVM, from the call site) methodType(Supplier::class.java), // 3. factory type (JVM, from the call site) methodType(Any::class.java), // 4. erased interface type (static argument) lookup.findStatic(Owner::class.java, "banner", methodType(String::class.java)), // 5. body methodType(String::class.java), // 6. instantiated type (static argument) ) @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") val s = site.target.invoke() as Supplier<String>

recap: invokedynamic names a method name, a type and a bootstrap method. The bootstrap method runs once per call site and returns a CallSite; afterwards the instruction calls its target directly.
A lambda is a private body method plus an invokedynamic. The call-site type lists the captured values, and LambdaMetafactory makes a hidden $$Lambda class at first use.
Capturing nothing gives one shared instance; capturing gives a new object per evaluation, all of one class. Reading a field captures this.

String + (JDK 9+) and Kotlin templates (JVM target 9+) use StringConcatFactory.makeConcatWithConstants with a \u0001 recipe. Records use ObjectMethods.bootstrap; pattern switches use SwitchBootstraps, and enum labels in them use condy.
Kotlin lambdas use invokedynamic by default since Kotlin 2.0, inline functions such as forEach create no lambda at all, and a function reference became a generated class in this track's build.
The limit: every call site links to a method that already exists. To make a whole new class that implements an interface while the program runs, you need the next lesson's dynamic proxies.

explain.prompt: Explain to a teammate what happens, from javac to the first call, when Java code says IntUnaryOperator later = s -> s + extra;, and why the second time the line runs is cheaper than the first.
explain.answer: javac moves the body into a private static method, lambda$...$0(int extra, int s), with the captured extra first. Where the lambda appears, it emits an invokedynamic whose type is (I)IntUnaryOperator, plus a BootstrapMethods entry that points at LambdaMetafactory.metafactory with the erased interface type, the body and the instantiated type. The first time the line runs, the JVM calls the metafactory, which makes a hidden $$Lambda class whose applyAsInt calls the body, and returns a ConstantCallSite whose target constructs that class. The JVM links the instruction to it. The second time, there's no bootstrap call and no class to make: the instruction calls the target, which allocates one small object holding extra. If the lambda captured nothing, the target would just return the same instance every time.

deeper.html:
Condy is easy to see. Compile this with javac 21 or later and run javap -v:

Java
sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square {}
record Circle(int r) implements Shape {}
enum Square implements Shape { UNIT }

static String name(Shape s) {
    return switch (s) {
        case Circle c -> "circle " + c.r();
        case Square.UNIT -> "unit square";
    };
}
Kotlin
// kotlinc compiles this `when` to an instanceof check and an enum comparison: no typeSwitch
sealed interface Shape
data class Circle(val r: Int) : Shape
enum class Square : Shape { UNIT }

fun name(s: Shape) = when (s) {
    is Circle -> "circle ${s.r}"
    Square.UNIT -> "unit square"
}

The switch becomes invokedynamic typeSwitch:(Ljava/lang/Object;I)I with SwitchBootstraps.typeSwitch. Among its static arguments is a Dynamic constant-pool entry, shown as invoke:Ljava/lang/Enum$EnumDesc;, whose own bootstrap is ConstantBootstraps.invoke applied to Enum$EnumDesc.of. The enum label is built lazily, the first time the switch needs it, instead of forcing Square to initialize when the class loads.

The lambda factory changed tools recently. At jdk-23-ga, InnerClassLambdaMetafactory imports the JDK's internal copy of ASM, a library for writing class files; at jdk-24-ga it imports java.lang.classfile. Your class files didn't change at all. That's the point of invokedynamic: the JDK swapped its strategy underneath, and every lambda compiled since Java 8 picked it up.
